subject: mathematics
question_text: If f(x) = x² and g(x) = 2ˣ, solve (fog)(x) = (gof)(x).

verification.note: Source: Sri Chaitanya, FAST TRACK IPE for Jr. Students — Mathematics-IA (2026-27 edition), book p.11, chapter 2 FUNCTIONS, Very Short Answer question 14. Only the question was taken. The solution, the step order and the mark split are this answer book's own work — see docs/ORIGINALITY_MATHS.md. THE MARK SPLIT IS OURS, NOT THE BOOK'S: the Mathematics-IA volume prints no per-step mark allocation on any answer. The 1+1 split rewards writing both compositions first and equating the powers to reach the two roots second. Paper position: Maths-1A Section A runs Q1–Q10 at 2 marks each, all compulsory. This is a coaching publication, not a TSBIE document, so the split stays unverified until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms it. The third step, which puts both roots back into the original equation, carries no mark and is authored for the student, not for the examiner.

recall_prompt: Say how you would solve this — the two compositions, how the powers are compared, and the values of x.

page_header: Section A — Very Short Answer Question

steps.label: Write both compositions
steps.margin_note: First mark. Write both sides before solving anything. In fog, g acts first; in gof, f acts first, and that is the whole difference.

accept: f o g is two to the x all squared which is two to the two x
g o f is two to the power x squared
one side is two to the two x and the other is two to the x squared
fog lo g modata so two power two x, gof lo two power x square

steps.why: The two sides differ only in which function acts first, and that changes the power from 2x to x². Writing both compositions is what turns the question into an equation.
steps.memory_tip: (2ˣ)² = 2²ˣ, while 2 raised to x² stays 2^(x²). The two are not the same.
common_mistakes: Writing (2ˣ)² as 2^(x²), which would make both sides equal for every x.
Applying f first in fog, which swaps the two sides.

steps.label: Equate the powers and solve
steps.margin_note: Second mark. Same base on both sides, so the powers can be equated. Factorise instead of dividing by x, or the root x = 0 is lost.
lines: Same base, so the powers are equal:

recall.must_convey: That equal bases give 2x = x², which factorises to x(x − 2) = 0, so x = 0 or x = 2.
accept: same base so two x equals x squared
x squared minus two x equals zero so x into x minus two is zero
the roots are zero and two
base same kabatti powers equate cheyyali x zero or two
factorise and get x equals zero or x equals two

steps.why: Two powers of the same base are equal only when the powers are equal, so the exponential equation becomes a quadratic. Factorising keeps both roots; dividing by x would lose x = 0.
steps.memory_tip: Never divide by x to solve x² = 2x. Move everything to one side and factorise, so x = 0 is not lost.
common_mistakes: Dividing both sides by x and giving only x = 2.
Factorising x² − 2x as x(x + 2) and giving the roots 0 and −2.

steps.label: Check both roots
steps.margin_note: No mark of its own. Both values are put back into the original equation, which is how the student sees that neither root is extraneous.

recall.must_convey: That both x = 0 and x = 2 satisfy the original equation, so the solution set is {0, 2}.
accept: at x equals zero both sides give one
at x equals two both sides give sixteen
both roots satisfy the equation so the solution set is zero and two
rendu roots correct so solution set zero and two
check both values in the original equation

steps.why: Equating the powers is a reversible step here, so no extra root appears — but putting both values back is the only way to show it rather than assume it.
steps.memory_tip: Put every root back into the original equation. Here 0 and 2 both give the same value on each side.
common_mistakes: Checking one root only and assuming the other one works too.
Stopping at x² = 2x without writing the roots.
